#10577. The next big creators will be experts

When I started hosting a podcast this year, I assumed the guests whose message would travel furthest would be the ones with the biggest followings. That’s how I’d been taught to think about talent for 20 years, since the MySpace days, but it turned out to be the other way round.

One clip of the Irish Nigerian author Emma Dabiri, explaining with care how the language of race was invented, passed a million views on its own. Another of the most shared conversations was with Clare Rewcastle Brown, an unassuming British journalist who broke the 1MDB scandal in Malaysia from a spare room with a blog and a shortwave radio and watched the prime minister at the center of it end up in prison.

Neither woman is trying to be famous, and that seems to be the point. After a decade of feeds tuned to whoever is best at being watched, audiences are hungry for people who actually know things. I think it’s a direct reaction to how much of what we scroll past now is confident, polished, and empty. The people who have spent decades on the slow work are suddenly the ones traveling fastest, and that should change who brands pay to speak for them.

None of this is an argument against the creator economy, which has become the engine room of modern marketing. Unilever’s chief executive talks about building an “army of creators,” and the company now works with close to 300,000 of them, up from around 10,000 two years ago. Coca-Cola took 10,000 to the Paris Olympics, and well over 200 million people now describe themselves as one. At Cannes Lions this June you couldn’t move along the Croisette without someone pushing a little furry mic into a stranger’s face.

15 minutes of fame

Andy Warhol promised everyone 15 minutes of fame, but our feed went one better and made everyone a creator for 15 seconds, which sounds wonderfully democratic until you try to tell any of them apart. A decade ago a face talking to camera was the antidote to corporate advertising, the human touch that made a brand feel like a friend’s recommendation. Multiply that by a few hundred thousand, add AI presenters who never age, never sleep, and never fluff a line, and the human face starts to blur into its own kind of slop, the same beige vanilla texture that has already swallowed most of the timeline.

What cuts through is a story told by somebody who was actually there, which is the one thing a machine can’t claim.

We describe the show I host as extraordinary stories, told by the people who lived, or found them, and the more episodes we make, the more that second half matters. Trust in news fell to 37% this year, the lowest the Reuters Institute has recorded since it began measuring in 2015. In a post-truth climate, the qualities audiences reward are the old reporter’s virtues: knowing where a fact came from and having a proper answer to why anyone should care. Two middle-aged historians talking for an hour at a time on The Rest Is History now pull around 30 million downloads and streams a month, and seven in 10 of their listeners are under 40. That’s about as far from what we assumed Insta culture wanted as it’s possible to get.

The expert economy

If we have to give it a name I’d call it the expert economy, where the experts become the new rock stars and we have never needed them more. When anybody can generate a convincing explanation of anything in a few seconds, the people who actually know become the most valuable voices. Truth is starting to behave like a premium tier the way you pay Spotify to make the ads go away, and the only people who can supply it are the ones who’ve spent their lives checking.

This also brings back a figure some spent 15 years trying to automate away, the editor. The feed was supposed to make taste redundant, like a sort of algorithm of last resort choosing on our behalf. Our time-poor lives and continual quest for convenience meant most of us went along with whatever our algorithmic overlords served up.

But now the dam is breaking, and as we tire of these little screen dictators people are going back to a human editor of choice, someone whose judgment they’ve learned to trust over years of receipts and first-hand evidence. Brands have spent fortunes renting audiences from influencers, and very few have thought to back the judgment itself.

Some of the best voices around right now are really double acts. One half has spent 40 years on a single subject and is well past the age when the industry usually stops calling them, while the other half is a 25-year-old producer who knows how to cut one clip so it moves round the world at the speed of a meme. Together I think these new creative duos will make age more irrelevant, because the person who knows the most no longer has to be the person who understands the format.

What to look for

So here are four things I’d look for when backing an expert voice.

  • Look for the obsession that came before the audience. Clare Rewcastle Brown was writing about Borneo’s disappearing rainforest long before anyone was listening.
  • Ask for the whole hour. Almost anyone can hold your attention for 15 seconds but the people worth backing get more interesting the longer they’re allowed to talk, so maybe judge them on their longest conversation rather than their best clip.
  • Footnotes are king now. Sources, caveats, and the balls to say “I don’t know” have become some of the strongest trust triggers in media today and audiences are seeking this.
  • Book the people who’ll argue with your brief, not say yes to everything. An expert who agrees with everything you said has stopped being an expert and become an influencer again.

If a government can lose to one woman with a blog and a shortwave radio, every marketer should think for a moment. Reach these days can be bought by the yard but belief is earned by the decade. The people who’ve already put the decades in are sitting right there and many of them are mostly unbooked. 

The new expert economy might just be about to explode.

Supported Gemini Intelligence features on Motorola Signature 27 include:

Radeon drivers may be quietly racking up thousands of gigabytes in SSD writes

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An SSD can spend most of its day doing very little, particularly when a PC is sitting idle. That may not be the case for some AMD Radeon systems, however, with reports suggesting that AMD’s External Events Utility (EEU), which is installed alongside Radeon drivers, may be writing data to the system driver continuously, even when the computer is barely being used. The issue drew attention again on November 8, when Reddit user ‘darklinkpower’ highlighted reports of the unusual drive activity.

One Radeon owner claimed the problem had been quietly eating into their drive's reported health for more than a year, writing: "I just found out that the driver eats up 1% of my SSD health every month for 16 months." Another user reported sustained writes of approximately 5MB/s while their PC was idle. Another one claimed their SSD health had dropped by about 1% every month for 16 months. AMD has acknowledged the problem. In an October 21 response on its community forum, a company representative confirmed that they were investigating. “Yes. We're looking into it with the aim to resolve it in a future driver release." He said. Another representative, AMAD Vik, subsequently offered a more encouraging update on Reddit, apologizing and saying, “This is hopefully fixed in the next one."

Notably, the EEU is not an entirely unfamiliar culprit. Last November, a similar issue involving AMD chipset drivers arose, with a Redditor claiming he had discovered that the software repeatedly updated a log file whenever on-screen elements were moved or resized. That incident also prompted questions about whether stopping the service would affect FreeSync. The latest reports are a different proposition, though, with some users now seeing writes that barely let up, even when their PCs are doing nothing.

The numbers are worth looking at. At 5 MB/s, an SSD would receive about 18GB of host writes per hour. Over a full day, that's 432GB, and a month of uninterrupted activity could push the figures close to 13TB. That, however, does not necessarily mean being written to the NAND flash itself. SSD controllers use caching and wear-leveling, and other techniques, to manage incoming data. How much of that reported activity thus translates into actual flash wear is still unknown. The user's claim of losing 1% of drive health each month also hasn't been independently confirmed.

Moreover, there doesn't appear to be clear patterns across Radeon driver versions. Reports include systems running Adrenalin 26.19.2, as well as older releases, suggesting the problem may not be limited to the latest update. AMD's October 30 release notes for Adrenalin 26.20.2 don't mention the issue either. For now, it's difficult to say which driver versions, hardware combinations, or system configurations are responsible.

That said, there are two reported workarounds. The first involves opening the Windows Services application by pressing Win + R, entering services.msc, and locating AMD EEU. Users can then stop the service or change its startup type to Disabled. That appears to stop excessive writeups, but isn’t necessarily a clean solution. The second workaround involves disabling Resizable Bar (ReBAR), which another user reported had stopped the disk activity without disabling the EEU. This, however, isn’t ideal either, as ReBAR can improve gaming performance by allowing the PC to access the GPU’S memory more efficiently.

For now, checking whether the problem actually exists on your PC is probably the most sensible first step. Open Windows Resource Monitor by pressing Win + R, typing resmon, and selecting the Disk tab. Sort by write activity and look for sustained writes from atieclxx.exe or atiesrxx.exe. AMD has indicated that a fix is in the works, but hasn’t published a confirmed release date. Until then, Radeon owners may want to monitor their storage activity rather than immediately disabling driver services or changing BIOS settings.

#10574. Are stores open on Veterans Day 2026? Holiday hours for banks, stock markets, USPS, Walmart, Costco, and more

Since America’s creation 250 years ago, countless brave individuals have been willing to fight for it. Every November 11, the United States honors its veterans.

This year, the observance falls on a Wednesday, which is a little confusing. Here’s the rundown of why many get a day off in the middle of the week and what you can expect to be opened and closed for it.

Why isn’t Veterans Day always on a Monday?

Veterans Day is always on November 11 because of its links to World War I. The “Great War” was supposed to be the war to end all wars. If only that was the case.

On November 11, 1918, Germany and the Allied forces agreed to an armistice and stopped fighting. This agreement began on the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month. The Treaty of Versailles made the end of the war official about 14 months later.

The Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968 moved most holidays to Mondays to give workers a three-day weekend.

When it went into effect in 1971, Veterans Day was officially part of the shift. Backlash from veterans groups caused the holiday to be moved back to its historical roots.

Will the post office be open on Veterans Day? Will mail be delivered?

No and no. The United States Postal Service (USPS) will be closed and no regular mail will be delivered on Veterans Day because it is a federal holiday.

Are FedEx and UPS open on Veterans Day?

Physical FedEx locations will be open. However, deliveries and pick-ups will have some modifications. Early on-call pickups and drop box pickups may be impacted in some regions.

UPS is open for business as usual.

Are banks open on Veterans Day?

No, most banks will be closed. This includes major chains like Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo. Online banking and outdoor ATMs will be available for immediate needs.

Is the stock market open on Veterans Day?

Yes, both the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and the Nasdaq will be open on Veterans Day.

However, the U.S. bond market follows the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (SIFMA) calendar and will be closed.

Are schools open on Veterans Day?

It is best to check in with your child’s school to see if it will be open or closed on Veterans Day. Schools are run at the local level, so it is location dependent in many cases. Private institutions also have greater freedom in scheduling.

Are pharmacies open on Veterans Day?

Yes. Most major pharmacies are open on Veterans Day, including major chains like CVS and Walgreens.

It is always a good practice to double check before heading out just in case so you don’t get an even bigger headache.

Are retail stores, groceries, and restaurants open on Veterans Day?

The majority of retail stores and restaurants will remain open on Veterans Day. Big-box chains like Walmart and Target will be open. Membership-based retailers like Costco are also open on Veterans Day.

Grocery store chains like Kroger and Whole Foods are also open on Veterans Day.

What about Veterans Day freebies and deals?

Some restaurants are offering freebies and discounts for those who have served. Applebee’s is offering vets who dine in a free entree with seven options to choose from and a $5 coupon for future visits.

Vets and active military personnel with a sweet tooth can head to BJ’s Restaurant and Brewhouse for a free Chocolate Chunk Pizookie. As an added bonus, the establishment will also present these brave souls with a free appetizer coupon.

Participating Farmer Boys locations are offering vets and active military personnel a free Big Cheese Burger with proof of service.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When developing a website, developers often rely on CSS classes to style buttons, forms, navigation elements, and other interface components. This approach works well, but some situations require styles to depend on an element's HTML attributes rather than additional class names.

CSS attribute selectors provide a practical solution. They allow developers to target elements based on whether an attribute exists, what value it contains, or whether its value matches a particular pattern. Used carefully, they can simplify styling and make reusable components easier to maintain.

An attribute selector targets an HTML element using square brackets. For example, a developer can select every input field that has a required attribute:

This rule applies to inputs with the required attribute, regardless of their input type.

Developers can also target a specific attribute value:

This is useful when different input types need different visual treatments without introducing additional classes into the HTML.

Forms are a practical place to apply attribute selectors because HTML already provides attributes that describe how individual fields behave.

Consider a registration form containing email, password, and telephone fields. Each input can be styled according to its purpose:

The CSS can target these fields independently:

This approach keeps the markup descriptive while allowing the stylesheet to respond to the attributes already present in the document.

One important distinction is that required indicates a validation requirement, while :invalid represents an input's current validity state. These should not be treated as interchangeable.

CSS provides several matching operators that help developers target more specific attribute values.

These operators can be useful when working with links, downloadable files, language attributes, and reusable components.

For example, a website might want to distinguish PDF downloads from ordinary navigation links:

This adds a small visual indicator to links whose URLs end in .pdf.

Attribute selectors can also help identify links with different destinations or behaviors.

For example, external links that use HTTPS can receive a subtle visual indicator:

However, matching an HTTPS URL does not necessarily prove that a link points to an external website. Internal links can also use HTTPS, so developers should consider the actual navigation requirements before applying special styling.

For more examples of selector combinations and matching rules, SitePoint's guide to CSS Attribute Selectors provides a useful reference.

Although attribute selectors are flexible, they should not replace every class-based styling decision.

A selector such as [class*="button"] can match unintended elements if their class names happen to contain the same text. Similarly, broad attribute rules may affect components that were not originally intended to receive those styles.

For predictable results, use exact attribute matching whenever possible and prefer descriptive classes for major component styling.

Developers should also remember that CSS selectors only control presentation. They do not replace JavaScript validation, server-side security checks, or proper HTML semantics.

The MDN documentation on attribute selectors provides further details about selector syntax, matching behavior, and supported operators.

Before adding attribute selectors to a large stylesheet, inspect the affected elements using browser developer tools.

Check whether the selector matches the intended elements.

Test fields with different attribute values.

Verify disabled, required, and invalid form states.

Check navigation links and downloadable files.

Test the layout on mobile and desktop screens.

Review whether existing component styles are being unintentionally overridden.

This process helps identify unexpected matches before they affect the production interface.

CSS attribute selectors give developers another way to create flexible and maintainable interfaces without adding unnecessary classes to every HTML element.

They are particularly useful for form styling, link identification, and components that already contain meaningful HTML attributes. By choosing precise selectors, understanding matching operators, and testing changes before deployment, developers can use this feature to write cleaner CSS while keeping their markup descriptive and organized.

#10570. How Portland is spending its tax on billion-dollar companies

On a former landfill in Portland, Oregon, workers are installing hundreds of solar panels in a community solar project that will help people living nearby save on their electric bills. The new solar farm was funded by an unusual source: the city’s pioneering tax on billion-dollar corporations, which was enacted in November 2018 and has raised more than $1.7 billion to fund hundreds of climate-related projects.

The first-of-its-kind program, created through a citizen-led ballot measure, charges a 1% tax on the local retail sales of large corporations like Amazon and Walmart. The city hasn’t disclosed which companies have to pay, but it applies to corporations with more than $1 billion in annual retail sales and at least $500,000 in sales within Portland city limits, with some exemptions for necessities like groceries. Around 500 large companies are affected, and the revenue goes both to community grants and larger city projects, with a focus on climate justice.

Turning a landfill into a community asset

In the case of the solar farm, around 170 low-income families can sign up to use a portion of the electricity that’s generated. Because the city fund is covering the cost of putting in the solar panels, the project immediately creates steep savings for those customers—as much as 40% less than what people were paying on their utility bills before.

“Without those funds, it wouldn’t exist,” says Jessica Carmona, the renewables program director at the Bonneville Environmental Foundation, a nonprofit working on the project. “It’s not possible to build these types of sites for nonprofits that are low-income benefiting, with such high levels of savings, if you’re not getting funding.”

The solar farm sits on land now owned by the nonprofit Bird Alliance of Oregon, which is using another grant from the city fund to restore wildlife habitat on the former landfill. A high school across the street has gotten grants for youth climate action. On the same street, the city has used grant money to plant trees to help reduce extreme heat, and another grant will help fund a major new rapid bus corridor.

From a ‘bike bus’ to clean energy retrofits

Changes are rolling out throughout Portland, thanks to grants from the Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits Fund, which administers the revenue from the 1% tax. The latest round of grants includes expanding a “bike bus” program to help kids get to school safely on bikes—with the goal to ultimately help replace more than half a million miles in car trips to school—and another program that lets employees at a local university borrow bikes for their commute to work.

Other grants support access to EVs. Another Bird Alliance grant is expanding a program that works with homeowners to restore habitat in their backyards, creating a network that connects to parks; while it helps wildlife, it’s also adding shade and helping clean the air for people.

“What [the Portland Clean Energy Fund] is allowing us to do is to work with a total of 420 new households focused in areas that have the greatest burdens of urban heat islands and air pollution and low tree canopy,” says Micah Meskel, the director of conservation and rehabilitation at the Bird Alliance of Oregon. At its core, Meskel says, the city fund is a climate justice program. He argues that it’s fitting that corporations “who have the most negative impact on climate change be the ones that are paying for it.” The Bird Alliance, along with other nonprofits in the city, helped fight for the original ballot measure after seeing a need for more funding to tackle the growing impacts of climate change.

Grant money is also helping retrofit homes to reduce energy bills, and training workers to perform energy audits. The grants have helped the city respond to climate impacts that are happening faster than expected—after a deadly heat wave in 2021, for example, grants helped residents get air conditioners so they can be more resilient as extreme heat becomes more frequent. Several grants support new net-zero housing, which is housing that produces as much renewable energy as it consumes. The funding helps ensure that builders include features like heat pumps in homes even as the overall cost of construction keeps rising.

“We’re far too often in this environment where costs are going up tremendously and everyone is trying to figure out how do we get our housing built—which is so critical for our community—and they’re whittling away everything that they originally put into the plan,” says Sam Baraso, program manager for the Portland Clean Energy Fund. Heat pumps or extra insulation might get cut, he says, but the fund can help keep them in place.

As the Trump administration slashed federal funding across climate-related projects, Portland’s surcharge on billion-dollar companies helped it keep going. “There was an expectation that there were going to be other dollars for other things like electric vehicles and clean energy,” says Raffaele Timarchi, external affairs manager for the Portland Clean Energy Fund. “And when that stuff bottomed out at the federal and state level, we became the only game in town.” Several projects wouldn’t have moved forward, he says, if the fund hadn’t existed.

More money than expected

Corporations, unsurprisingly, fought the ballot measure when it was introduced, and the opposition campaign—with backing from Amazon and others—raised more money than the campaign in support. But it passed with a decisive 65% of the vote. (A later survey, in 2024, found that 65% of citizens had a favorable view of the fund.) The Portland Metro Chamber, a local business organization that had opposed the original ballot measure, defended it last year when questions arose about how the funds should be spent.

Soon after the climate fee took effect, two large supermarket chains added 1% charges to some non-food items in Portland stores. Customers sued the stores and won a settlement. It’s not clear whether any other companies have tried to pass on the cost in retail prices. But that likely has happened, says Eric Fruits, an economist who teaches at Portland State University who opposed the program. “Just naturally, it gets passed on,” he says. “Even if it’s not a line item, it’s going to get passed on in higher prices.” Any impacts have been hidden by inflation over the years since the program started, he says, though he believes that it didn’t ultimately do any real harm to consumers or retailers.

An early report from Portland’s city auditor in 2022 cited challenges with how the program was run, including a lack of clear goals to weak oversight of the effectiveness of the grants. A year later, the auditor found that the program had made progress, though management of the novel program still had room for improvement.

The team acknowledges that the program hasn’t been easy to build from scratch. “No one’s ever done this before, and sometimes it’s hard to make the road by walking,” says Timarchi. The law faced immediate challenges. After it went into place, the state passed a law that banned other communities from passing similar surcharges on the gross receipts of large businesses, though Portland got an exemption. As the nascent program began, planning also took time. The organizers recognized that the nonprofits they worked with would need time to build their own programs, and multiyear grants to make those programs last.

The funding also ended up being much larger than expected. The city had initially projected that the surcharge would generate up to $60 million a year; instead, it’s bringing in around $200 million a year. According to the city economist, one of the reasons was that the pandemic shifted shopping habits, and online retailers are selling more in Portland than they previously did; inflation also increased the dollar value of purchases. This meant that the program had to rethink how the money would be used. It expanded from community grants to also include funding for larger programs in the city.

“We have also seen great benefit in its evolution to bring in the city as an important partner to really scale the impact, especially within the built landscape and the sort of the set infrastructure of the city, whether it’s its park systems, its tree canopy, its transportation systems,” says the Bird Alliance’s Meskel. “It’s really tough for an individual organization or an individual to have an impact in those spaces. But when a jurisdiction takes a holistic approach to change a system, it can be really profound.”

As the money came in, there have been arguments about how it could be used. One ballot initiative this year, which failed, wanted to use some of the fund to pay for more police officers, not clean energy. As other cities consider similar programs (including Eugene, Oregon, which passed a related program this year), the Portland team says that it’s important to be clear about the goals and how the community will decide what gets funded.

And though the fund has had a visible impact, it’s still not enough for the city’s climate goals. “$1.6 billion that we moved over five years is just an illusion of abundance,” says Timarchi. “We’re a part of every energy efficient housing project that comes out of the city, nearly every green infrastructure project, urban forestry and beyond, and [transportation]. It’s just not enough money for all those projects, so this question of prioritization is really important.”

So far, the city estimates that the first three rounds of grants helped reduce around 25,500 metric tons of CO2 emissions. That’s a tiny amount in the context of the world’s 38 billion metric tons of emissions each year. But their impact can go beyond the emissions they directly prevent if it helps accelerate a broader shift toward lower-carbon ways of living. The grants are also making neighborhoods more resilient at a time when the risk of extreme heat keeps growing.

#10568. Sony revives the Walkman’s iconic MDR-3 headphones with USB-C for $60

Sony is bringing back its iconic Walkman MDR-3 headphones for the modern era with a USB-C connection and a price tag of $60.

Originally launched in 1979, Sony’s MDR-3 headphone lineup served as a companion to the Walkman cassette player and, now, they’re making a comeback. The Sony MDR-3R headphones are a USB-C revival of the classic design, just with connectivity that actually works on modern devices.

The design, Sony says, is a “faithful recreation” of the original and comes with blue or orange ear pads. Even the packaging and included manual “inherit the design of the original model.” As for the actual sound quality, Sony has “re-engineered” the same 23mm driver with sound “close to the original,” though refined for modern sound.

Along with the USB-C connection, they also feature a microphone and in-line remote, and Sony incorporated recycled plastic too.

Sony MDR-3R are available starting today for $59.99 from typical retailers.

Celebrating the Walkman’s role in Netflix’s Stranger Things, Sony is also releasing a red/black variant to match the ones worn by Max in the show. Those will cost $79.99.

Interaxon, the Canadian firm behind the Muse sleep and meditation headband, is one of them. Its devices monitor electrical activity in the brain, alongside other physiological measurements, while users sleep. The recordings are processed into reports that help customers track their rest and identify changes in their sleeping patterns. But there is another use for that information. Interaxon has already trained an AI model using about 50,000 hours of EEG recording and says it removes identifying information, including names, email, and addresses, before using the data. “We aim to use as much of that eligible corpus as possible,” Nadia Kumentas, its Chief Marketing Officer, said.

Notably, the idea behind these systems is particularly different from training a large language model. Instead of feeding AI an enormous amount of text, developers supply it with recordings of electrical activity in the brain. The model then learns recurring patterns that can be adapted to recognize different brain states or assist with specific research tasks. And there are already some interesting results. AI startup Piramidal has trained its model on more than 4 million hours of EEG data in partnership with Cleveland Clinic. The company developed a seizure-detection system that correctly identified nine out of 10 seizures in a pilot study after being fine-tuned on the clinic's recordings. That, however, doesn’t mean consumer headbands can suddenly read people's thoughts. Most wearable EEG devices use just one to six electrodes, considerably fewer than 19 to 25 typically found in clinical EEG systems. Also, their recordings are generally less comprehensive.

The industry has also been gathering neural recordings on a considerable scale. Last December, we covered Coundit’s effort to collect 10,000 hours of neural data from thousands of patients. The San Francisco startup built its own headset system to capture brain activity alongside speech and text, with the aim of developing AI capable of translating signals into language. Meta has also been working on BrainQwerty, a non-invasive brain-computer interface that translates brain activity into keyboard inputs. Its second-generation system improved average word accuracy to 61% from 40% in the earlier version, although the technology remains a far cry from practical everyday use.

#10566. A gilded tribute to Trump’s bone spurs appears on the National Mall

Just in time for Veterans Day, a new installation on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., pokes fun at one of President Donald Trump’s Vietnam War draft deferments.

The Foot Soldier depicts a seated and gilded Trump with one shoe off as he looks at his bare foot. According to The Secret Handshake, the anonymous art collective behind the statue, the piece was inspired by the idea of what a Lincoln Memorial-style sculpture of Trump might look like. “We wanted it to have a regal, military feel,” the group says in an email. But unlike Lincoln, who is depicted gazing pensively into the distance, Trump is focused entirely on himself (of course).

Made of foam, plastic, wood, and rebar, the temporary statue is located at Madison Drive NW between 7th and 9th streets, opposite the National Gallery of Art Sculpture Garden. It will remain on display through Veterans Day, Wednesday, November 11.

The Secret Handshake is also behind previous installations on the National Mall that criticized Trump’s friendship with Jeffrey Epstein, his handling of the Iran war, and his taste in interior design. Each satirizes the president’s ethical shortcomings. This time, the collective took aim at the president’s dereliction of duty.

Trump received multiple draft deferments during the Vietnam War, including one in 1968 at age 22 for bone spurs in his heels. He said in 2016 that he received “a very strong letter on the heels.” The daughter of a podiatrist who rented office space in a building owned by Trump’s father claimed in 2018 that her dad gave the future president the diagnosis as a favor for the elder Trump.

The installation mocks the so-called diagnosis. A plaque on the statue’s base reads: “We honor the service and sacrifice of our Commander in Chief, Donald J. Trump. He’s a soldier in spirit, who marched to the front lines of dodging the draft, armed with a perfect diagnosis of bone spurs. We salute a leader who knows you can’t spell sacrifice without ‘I,’ and a warrior who reminds us that sometimes when you’re called to stand up, it’s best to just sit down and rest your feet.”

The statue also includes a quote from Trump—“I can be very military”—which is pulled from a 2013 Facebook post he shared of his parents and him during his time at the New York Military Academy in Cornwall. In the photo, Trump is wearing his dress uniform.

For this sculpture, the collective added an interactive element, a 6-foot-tall bone spur mascot named “Toey.” In an email, the group said they added a mascot to “feel silly and celebratory. He’s there to amp up the absurdity and interact with people.”

Trump has long received criticism over his deferment. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), an Iraq War veteran, has called him “Cadet Bone Spurs” on multiple occasions. And former Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, a retired four-star U.S. Marine general who served during Trump’s first term, said this in 2019: “I earned my spurs on the battlefield . . . Donald Trump earned his spurs in a letter from a doctor.” Now the new statue and mascot give jokes about Trump’s bone spurs a visual punch line.

#10564. Personalizing everything doesn’t mean people feel seen

When a young employee was given options for a gift by her employer, she didn’t choose a candle, a journal, or a day at the spa. Instead, she chose to donate the funds to pay for cancer patients’ rides to their treatment centers.

Her decision had a deeply personal connection: Her own mother was going through cancer treatment, and she knew how hard even simple logistics could become during an already difficult time.

Would an algorithm have predicted her choice, or the emotional significance behind it? Probably not.

AI can predict preferences, personalize communication, and automate interactions at a scale businesses couldn’t before. And in many cases, that’s incredibly useful. But as companies get better at anticipating what people might want, there’s a risk of confusing prediction with actually knowing someone.

As we embrace AI in an increasingly automated world, we should give just as much thought to the moments where human choice and attention still matter.

DON’T ASSUME YOU KNOW WHAT PEOPLE VALUE

Showing appreciation for customers, employees, and partners has long been an important business practice. And as in most areas of business, companies have relied on standardization to create consistency at scale. But scaling appreciation can sometimes have the opposite effect.

Not every person feels seen, recognized, or valued in the same way. When a company gives identical gifts to every customer who signs a renewal, for example, the company may believe it’s delighting those customers. But the gift won’t necessarily land that way for everyone. In fact, 70% of people have reported receiving a corporate gift they did not want.

The same is true for employees and partners. Recognizing everyone the same way isn’t necessarily the same as making everyone feel seen. Sometimes the more personal thing a company can do is ask.

PERSONALIZATION CAN MEAN PARTICIPATION

There’s no question that AI algorithms are becoming increasingly powerful. With more information, technology can get remarkably good at predicting what someone may want based on what it already knows about them.

But predictions aren’t always right. More importantly, there’s more to personalization than feeding someone’s past purchases or stated preferences into an algorithm.

There’s also participation: giving people a say in the experience itself. That might mean asking an employee what kind of recognition matters to them, letting a customer choose how they engage with a company, or giving someone options for how they’d like to be appreciated.

The next evolution of personalization may be more about knowing when to let people participate. The employee whose mother was going through cancer is a good example. Her company didn’t need to know that personal detail about her life to give her a meaningful gift. It just needed to give her a choice.

By allowing her to select something she would personally enjoy or direct those funds toward a cause she cared about, the company created room for her to bring her own meaning to the gesture.

GIFTING SHOWS THE DIFFERENCE

Corporate gifting is a particularly clear example because companies are constantly trying to make employees, customers, and partners feel appreciated through recognition programs, rewards, milestones, and gifts.

Instead of asking what to give them, the company might ask how to let them choose what feels meaningful.

We’ve seen firsthand that when people are given that agency, their choices can be surprising. Our research found that 81% prefer choosing their own gift, and in one campaign, roughly half chose a charitable gift rather than a physical item.

Someone may choose a traditional gift. Someone else may choose an experience. Another person may decide they’d rather turn that gift into support for a cause that matters to them. None of those choices is more correct than another, and that’s the point.

A business doesn’t always need to know enough about a person to predict the perfect gesture. Sometimes it needs to create enough flexibility for that person to make the gesture meaningful for themselves.

DON’T OPTIMIZE AWAY THE HUMAN PART

AI will continue making business faster, easier, and more personalized. But efficiency shouldn’t become the only measure of a good interaction.

A personal conversation or a thoughtful recognition, which might mean asking someone what they want and what they care about, can require more effort than an automated interaction. That extra effort is sometimes the cost of paying attention to another human being.

Even with more technology for predicting what people might want, the companies that make people feel most valued may be the ones that also know when not to guess.

Laura Hertz is CEO of Gifts for Good.

AAWireless is known for helping you convert a wired Android Auto connection into a wireless one, but the company is now launching a new product – an active-cooled Qi2 car charger.

Update 11/5: After debuting solely on the company’s website, AAWireless Charge is also now available on Amazon in the US.

“AAWireless Charge” is a Qi2 25W wireless car charger that costs $50. The charger is compatible with MagSafe, Pixelsnap, and Qi2 in general, and supports up to 25W charging speeds on compatible phones.

“Charge” also includes active cooling support with a built-in fan that the company says is “quiet” when active.

Included in the box you’ll find both an air vent mount as well as an adhesive base. There are also two magnetic ring adapters in the box for “Qi2 Ready” phones that don’t have magnets built-in or a magnetic case available. AAWireless says to use your car’s 12V outlet with the included adapter for “best performance,” but you can also use existing USB-C connections so long as they deliver enough power.

To be clear, there’s no wireless adapter built into the charger (as cool as that would be), but you can use this alongside an AAWireless adapter while driving, the company specifically mentions.

#10561. Democrats are back. So is economist Stephanie Kelton’s big idea

In the early days of the Biden administration, after the COVID-19 pandemic and overlapping recession, advocates of government spending to aid the recovery faced concerns that such programs would add to the seemingly ever-growing national debt. 

In addition to arguments about unemployment and the overall health of the economy, backers of spending bills like what became the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act had an increasingly influential economic idea on their side. Modern Monetary Theory, or MMT, arose from the work of numerous economists, but it was especially popularized by the work of Stephanie Kelton,  an economics professor who was a senior economic advisor to Senator Bernie Sanders’s presidential campaigns in 2016 and 2020 and served as chief economist for the Democratic staff of the Senate Budget Committee toward the end of the Obama administration. 

MMT, in essence, argues that deficit spending by governments with the power to issue their own currency isn’t inherently bad. And, as Kelton argued in her influential 2020 book The Deficit Myth, it can be used to promote a more prosperous and just economy. Common analogies between government deficit spending and consumers racking up credit card bills to spend beyond their means miss the mark, MMT’s advocates argue. 

“The work that I do explains why the federal government’s budget doesn’t work like a household budget, and why there is more capacity to spend on priorities, whether it’s healthcare, education, infrastructure, climate,” says Kelton. “Whatever it is, the spending capacity is there.” 

Since 2020, we’ve seen the end of the pandemic, the rise of inflation, and the reelection of Donald Trump, who despite pledges to shrink the size of government and limit international involvement has spent heavily on immigration enforcement and the war with Iran. Now, with a historic wave of Democrats set to take office in the House, Senate, and state governments across the country after campaigning on promises of affordability, MMT may again be poised to influence the direction of government. 

“I know that the book has been read, and the ideas have reached many of the candidates who are now getting prepared to take office in the Senate and House and across the country,” says Kelton, who today serves as a professor of economics and public policy at Stony Brook University, where she’s been based since 2017.   

‘Spending always has consequences’

One of the earliest academic proponents of what became known as MMT is L. Randall Wray, today a professor of economics at the Levy Economics Institute of Bard College. Kelton studied under Wray at the University of Denver early in her career, and the two were later both based at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where they were affiliated with the Center for Full Employment and Price Stability. At first, their research on monetary theory struggled to gain acceptance in the academic world, Wray says. 

“We had funding, so we could have conferences, and we wrote academic papers,” Wray says. “We gave presentations at academic conferences, and I can tell you none of that had an impact. We were trying to change the economic discipline, and it did not want to be changed.” 

What did help make a difference was a blog, New Economic Perspectives, founded by Kelton in time for both the 2000s blogosphere boom and the questioning of established economic wisdom in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and Great Recession. “I sort of thought it was a waste of time—this was very early in the blogosphere,” Wray recalls. “But the blog took off, and really, that’s how MMT got to be known.” 

New Economic Perspectives drew the attention of readers in both the formal economics world and beyond, sparking online debates with other prominent economists, including the Nobel laureate and longtime New York Times columnist Paul Krugman. “By the time Krugman heard about it, I don’t know the number, but I would say there were thousands of people in the blogosphere who understood MMT, and we didn’t need to debate Krugman because they would do it,” Wray says. 

In general, the academic researchers who developed and advocated MMT have been interested in communicating their ideas, says Pavlina R. Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College and president of the Levy Economics Institute.  

“A number of us engaged in this research project have spent a fair amount of time communicating some of these ideas to policymakers at the local and national level,” she says, as well as promoting their ideas to an expanding audience via social media and traditional news coverage so they could have influence beyond the confines of academic economics. 

“It started as an academic exercise that was always very closely connected to the idea that we can have good things; that we can secure full employment, greater economic well-being, and price stability,” says Tcherneva, who is also the author of The Case for a Job Guarantee. 

Over time, MMT found adherents in the Sanders campaign and elsewhere, where policymakers were discussing ways government spending could benefit the economy, even as they continued to face traditional questions about how various proposed programs could be funded. In general, there’s been a broad shift by Democrats and their allies in the direction of MMT over the past decade or so, says J.W. Mason, associate professor of economics at John Jay College and senior fellow at the Groundwork Collaborative. 

“People have much less concern about deficits as a constraint on policy than they had, you know, 15 or 20 years ago,” he says. “Over time, we got to something that looked much more like a vision of the world in which people recognize deficits are not the constraint that we had imagined that they were, and I think that Stephanie Kelton and MMT certainly contributed to that shift.” 

Of course, the Biden administration’s recovery spending was closely followed by a wave of inflation. Critics of MMT have argued essentially as long as the theory has been en vogue that its application would lead to inflation, with increased government spending driving up prices overall, and some have portrayed the post-pandemic burst of inflation as proving the theory dangerous and unreliable. 

But MMT advocates like Kelton, who served on a Biden-Sanders economic task force in 2020 that helped craft some of the early ideas around the relief programs, say the theory has always taken into account the fact that excessive spending can lead to inflation. She says she cautioned the Biden administration about this without success, including through a 2021 opinion piece in The New York Times. In essence, says Kelton, while the government can print money as needed, it can “run out of things to buy” if the resources of the economy, including labor and productive capacity, are stretched to their limits, driving up prices. 

“Spending always has consequences, and one of the consequences can be inflation,” says Kelton, who is working on a book challenging preconceptions of inflation. “And so the whole MMT project revolves around recognizing where the limits are.” 

Conversely, she says, some policies that might seem expensive can actually have a deflationary effect. Moving to a Medicare for All-style healthcare system, for instance, would likely increase government spending but could cut overall spending on healthcare by bringing costs more in line with those in other countries. That could lead to deflation and job losses if officials don’t take care to balance that spending elsewhere. 

‘It’s not an operating manual’

The new Congress may also be able to tackle inflation by reversing unpopular moves by the Trump administration; for instance, taking steps to curb tariffs and wind down the war with Iran.

“We were drifting back down toward 2% when the Trump administration walked through the door, and then we got immediately tariffs, and we got a war,” says Kelton, who continues a stream of public appearances and media interviews promoting her ideas and is a founding fellow at the Sanders Institute, the Vermont think tank cofounded by the senator’s wife, Jane O’Meara Sanders. 

While MMT has so far been more publicly embraced by Democrats, Kelton says the economic theory itself is more of a framework or lens that doesn’t itself call for any particular policy. Advocates of tax cuts, for example, might use the theory to understand their potential effect in the same way that those calling for increased spending on social programs might.  

“It’s not an operating manual that tells you pull this lever, turn this thing, do this policy,” says Kelton. “It’s just a framework, so you can apply that framework and say, oh, it looks like the economy has enough capacity that we could do some tax cuts.” 

And like many influential theories, MMT has arguably had an influence on political and economic discussions even when it’s not invoked by name, enabling discussions of potential government programs that aren’t dominated by concerns about funding and the national debt. 

“My sense is that during the Biden era, the pay-for question was not such a big obstacle, in part because the MMT conversation was everywhere,” says Tcherneva. “It almost provided breathing room for people to speak about bold policies—the Build Back Better agenda—that we will try and attempt big things without it being hamstrung by the pay-for question.” 

With incoming Congressional Democrats seemingly looking for ways to make everyday life more affordable, including restored spending on healthcare and food aid, it seems likely that some will turn to MMT for a theoretical understanding—and justification—of increased public spending, even if that requires borrowing. 

“I think you’re going to see a lot of elected Democrats come in looking for a very aggressive public spending program,” says Mason at the Groundwork Collective. “And I think it’s going to be helpful to have some strong arguments that the federal debt is not the main thing we should be thinking about at this moment.”

#10557. Pharma found its way into sports

If you’ve spent any Sunday this fall watching an NFL broadcast, you may have noticed a shift in the advertising landscape. Alongside the team logos between third-down stops and touchdown drives were cancer screening messages from Novartis, extending beyond national broadcasts into local stadiums across six NFL franchises. Meanwhile, if we look to Major League Baseball, AbbVie has established itself as MLB’s first official pharmaceutical partner, while also bringing its brain health awareness campaigns to the PGA Tour.

These partnerships represent a meaningful change for the pharmaceutical industry that, for decades, has approached sporting events only by purchasing television advertising during commercial breaks. Pharmaceutical companies now want to reach fans beyond traditional TV spots by becoming part of the sporting experience itself, building relationships with leagues, athletes, and audiences in ways that would have been unusual a decade ago.

The appeal of sports to the pharmaceutical industry is backed by numbers. Sporting events accounted for 96 of the 100 most-watched U.S. television broadcasts in 2025. That momentum continued into 2026, with NFL games averaging 18.8 million viewers through the first five weeks of the season, the highest average at this point in a season on record. At a time when audiences are increasingly fragmented across platforms, it’s rare to have such a large captive audience, explaining why brands are looking to establish a presence in professional sports.

RETHINK THE PARTNERSHIP APPROACH

As healthcare digital advertising spending continues to grow and the FDA takes a closer look at direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical marketing, companies are reassessing how they invest their advertising dollars. Beyond the audience size, the growth of women’s sports and greater openness among athletes about their mental and physical health have created opportunities for conversations that extend well beyond competition.

Yet while the industry’s growing presence in sports is encouraging, I worry that some pharmaceutical companies are approaching these partnerships with the same thinking that has long shaped traditional advertising—securing the audience first, then figuring out what to say.

Having spent much of my career in healthcare marketing, I’ve seen how easily a promising partnership can become an exercise in visibility rather than a strategy grounded in patients’ needs. Let’s say a company signs a recognizable athlete. Often, it’s not until after negotiating league sponsorship rights or investing in a high-profile activation that the company begins asking how the arrangement supports its broader business objectives. By that point, the investment has been made, and the pressure to justify it can become more important than determining whether it was the right decision.

AN OPPORTUNITY REQUIRING AUTHENTICITY

Sports organizations and athletes have a reliable “in” with communities that healthcare companies often struggle to reach through conventional advertising. These companies have an opportunity to address health topics that patients are often reluctant to discuss by harnessing the dedicated fan base loyalty and athlete credibility. But without a clear understanding of the healthcare challenges companies are trying to address, these partnerships risk becoming just another advertising opportunity, rather than a campaign built around the outcomes they hope to achieve.

Healthcare requires a different level of participation from athletes and spokespeople compared to typical consumer product endorsements. These campaigns often involve a sensitive diagnosis or personal medical decision. That requires a level of authenticity and vulnerability that can’t be manufactured through the usual advertising tactics. An athlete’s genuine experience with a health issue is much more likely to resonate than one where a recognizable name is just attached to a generic message.

HOW TO MEASURE SUCCESS

The advertising industry needs to change how it measures success for a worthwhile shift to occur. Metrics such as impressions, media coverage, brand awareness, and social engagement are standard for measuring campaign success. While measuring the reach is important, these numbers don’t reveal much, if anything, about whether a campaign has actually influenced health-related decisions. It shouldn’t be assumed that a partnership has improved access to care or encouraged patients to take action just because of these noted numbers attached to it.

Companies should be thinking from the start about how to assess and measure whether audiences sought additional information, discussed screening with a healthcare professional, or took steps toward scheduling an appointment. Not every outcome can be directly attributed to a sponsorship, but establishing those objectives before making an investment provides a more significant basis to evaluate its success.

Pharma has already demonstrated that it can buy its way into some of the biggest stages in professional sports. Whether it can turn that visibility into something valuable for patients will determine if these partnerships become a lasting part of healthcare marketing or simply another expensive way to compete for attention.

Ed Mitzen is the founder of Fingerpaint Group and The Business For Good Foundation.

#10556. How to Get a YouTube API Key and Use the Data API (2026)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You need a YouTube API key the moment your app has to read anything from YouTube: a video's length, its view count, a channel's latest uploads. Getting one takes about five minutes. Using it well takes a little longer, because YouTube changed how its quota works in June 2026, and plenty of guides still describe the old rules.

In this guide we'll get a key, lock it down and test it. Then we'll use it from Node.js for three real jobs: adding up the length of a playlist, listing a channel's videos without spending a search, and estimating what a video earned. Along the way we'll cover what the YouTube API costs (nothing), how the 2026 quota works, and the errors you're most likely to hit.

A YouTube API key identifies your project to the YouTube Data API v3. With just a key, you can read public data:

A key isn't enough for anything that touches someone's account. Uploading videos, editing playlists or reading private data needs OAuth 2.0, where the user signs in and grants your app access.

You'll need a Google account. The YouTube Data API is free, so there's nothing to pay for.

The restrictions matter more than they look. A key is just a string in a URL, and anyone who copies an unrestricted one can spend your daily quota for you. With an API restriction, the key is useless for other Google APIs. With an application restriction, it only works from your server or your site. Changes to restrictions can take up to five minutes to apply, so don't panic if a request fails straight after you save.

Before writing any code, check the key with a single request. This one asks for the first video ever uploaded to YouTube, and uses the fields parameter to trim the response down to four values:

That request cost 1 unit of your daily quota, which brings us to the question everyone asks.

Yes. There's no charge per request and no paid plan. Instead you get a daily quota, and since June 1, 2026 it's split into separate buckets:

Google's quota calculator lists the cost of every method. Quotas reset at midnight Pacific Time. Every request costs at least 1 unit, including requests that fail, so a retry loop around a broken call can use up a day's quota on its own.

If you've read older guides, search is the big change. A search used to cost 100 units out of the same 10,000, so 100 searches emptied your whole day. Uploads were worse still, at about 1,600 units each until December 2025. Now both have their own buckets, and the 10,000 units are left for everything else.

To give you a feel for what 10,000 units buys, here's what each example in this guide costs:

You can't pay for more. To go above the defaults, fill in the YouTube API Services Audit and Quota Extension Form, which is linked from Google's page on quota and compliance audits. YouTube first audits your project to check it follows the YouTube API Services Terms of Service, then someone from the API team gets back to you. Google doesn't give a timeline, so apply well before you need the extra quota.

Most projects never need to. The rest of this guide is about getting a lot done with very few units.

The examples need Node.js 20.6 or later, for the built-in fetch and the --env-file flag. There are no packages to install. Make a folder with a .env file in it:

Every example imports one small helper. It builds the URL, adds your key and turns API errors into readable messages:

Run any example with node --env-file=.env followed by the file name.

YouTube doesn't tell you how long a playlist is. To work it out, you need two methods:

Durations come back in ISO 8601 format. PT15M33S is 15 minutes 33 seconds, PT1H2M3S adds an hour, and a stream longer than a day looks like P1DT2H3M4S. The toSeconds() function below handles all three.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Full Courses in One Video playlist:

That's 184 hours of courses for 4 units of quota. Private and deleted videos still show up in a playlist's items, but videos.list doesn't return them, which is why the script prints "52 of 52 videos available". On a playlist with removed videos, the two numbers will differ.

This is the core of the free YouTube playlist length calculator I built on createthat.ai. The live version adds a target time box that works out the speed you need to finish by a deadline, and it accepts channel, video and Shorts links as well as playlists.

The obvious way to find a channel's videos is to search for them. Don't: search is now capped at 100 calls a day, and it isn't built to list everything a channel has posted. Every channel has an uploads playlist instead, and you can reach it in two cheap calls:

Two units, and none of your 100 daily searches. To get every upload rather than the newest five, page through the playlist with the same pageToken loop as Example 1.

videos.list with part=statistics returns a video's view, like and comment counts. Dislike counts have been private since December 2021 and favoriteCount is always 0, so don't build anything on those. The script also copes with a missing like or comment count, which you'll see on some videos.

This time the fields parameter trims the response to the values we use. That makes the response smaller, but it doesn't change the cost: the call is 1 unit either way.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Learn Python full course, one of the most-watched videos in that playlist:

Treat the last line as a rough range, not an answer. The Data API doesn't share anyone's revenue, so any estimate is views multiplied by an RPM: what a creator keeps per 1,000 views. RPM moves a lot with the topic and where the viewers live, and the estimate assumes the video shows ads, which not every channel does.

And sometimes you don't need an API at all. When I built a font tester, I needed a list of Google Fonts. The Google Fonts Developer API would have meant a key and a call on every visit, for a list that barely changes. Instead I generated a file of the 500 most popular fonts once, from Google's public font metadata, and the page loads it like any other file. No key, no quota and nothing to fail.

When a call fails, the response's error.message and error.details[0].reason tell you why. These are the ones you'll see most:

For the invalid key error, the full response looks like this:

Yes. Creating a key and calling the YouTube Data API costs nothing. You're limited by the daily quota instead, and there's no paid tier: more quota comes through an audit.

In the Google Cloud console, select your project and go to APIs & Services > Credentials. Your keys are listed under API keys, with a Show key option next to each one.

It works, but anyone can read the key from your page. If you do it, restrict the key to your website and to the YouTube Data API v3. A small server route that calls the API for you is safer, and it gives you somewhere to cache results.

By default, 100 searches, 100 uploads and 10,000 units for everything else. Most reads cost 1 unit and videos.list takes 50 IDs per call, so that's enough for the details of up to 500,000 videos a day.

Getting a YouTube API key is the easy part: one project, one API to enable, one key and two restrictions. The 2026 quota is generous if you work with it:

All three examples together cost 7 units, out of 10,000. From here, try commentThreads.list to pull a video's comments 100 at a time, or extend Example 2 to page through a channel's entire upload history and add it all up with the code from Example 1.

#10553. Why turning to AI for workplace support is backfiring

We’ve all been on a quest to make our workdays a little easier. For years, we’ve been adopting new tools, automating tedious tasks, and stripping away the barriers that slow us down. With AI, we’re closer to that frictionless day than ever before. Yet, in our rush to make work as smooth as possible (which, don’t get me wrong, I highly value), might we risk dissolving the social fabric that helps teams thrive? 

Workday’s recent research, the Human Connection Workplace Index, shows that 14% of employees overall, and 20% of Gen Z, have taken time off in the past year due to feelings of loneliness or isolation. 

To understand why efficiency doesn’t necessarily lead to well-being, I wanted to look closely at the work of Constance Hadley, PhD, an organizational psychologist and the founder of the Institute for Life at Work. She has spent years studying the drivers of employee isolation. Her empirical work on workplace loneliness demonstrates that true human connection is more complex than simply co-existing in a physical or digital workspace.

When I sat down to chat with Hadley about how emerging technologies intersect with workplace isolation, she captured our new reality perfectly: “We now have AI as a potential substitute for human connection, and it’s a new player in the relationship dynamic at work.”

THE AI SUPPORT PARADOX

In her most recent research, published in Harvard Business Review, Hadley found a trend. Three-quarters of regular AI users reported turning to AI for career coaching and friendship, support traditionally provided by colleagues. Strikingly, employees frequently described these tools as empathetic, patient, and nonjudgmental. However, half of these workers also reported feeling moderately or highly lonely on the job.

Workday’s research reinforces these findings, revealing that one-third of employees rarely or never have personal conversations with their colleagues, and one in five Gen Z employees say they feel lonelier since AI tools were introduced in the workplace. 

Both studies seem to point to the same realization: As technology becomes the path of least social resistance, the human interaction that builds cohesion might be fading away.

4 RELATIONAL RISKS



In her research, Hadley outlines four specific relational disruptions that occur when software replaces human collaboration. The first is when companies may downsize their workforce during restructuring. In this case, independent work may increase, leading to greater workplace isolation. 

The second is social stamina atrophy, when constantly interacting with a nonjudgmental and patient chatbot may make human conversations seem more intimidating or exhausting. In fact, our Workday research shows that, since the widespread adoption of AI, almost one-third of employees say they’re losing key social muscles as a result. These reports include at least one warning sign: less patience for small talk, trouble reading colleagues’ cues, heightened anxiety around unscripted check-ins, or a declining ability to resolve conflict face-to-face.

The third disruption happens when workers default to AI for answers rather than asking a peer, and therefore, opportunities to build trust and reciprocity disappear. 

Finally, the fourth disruption is what Hadley describes as an “existential loneliness” that’s triggered when you realize you are confiding in an artificial program, incapable of true presence. Her description of the illusion of intimacy reminds me of a point I once heard psychotherapist Esther Perel say, about how many people have hundreds of online “friends,” but no one to feed their cat when they go out of town. When your go-to confidant at work is an algorithm, that sense of solitude can be profound.

RETHINK OUR NEEDS

It’s also important not to miscalculate who is most at risk. During our conversation, Hadley shared a crucial insight regarding personality and social needs. She described loneliness as “the gap between what you’re seeking and what you’re getting back.” So, although we may often assume that introverts, for example, are thriving in this era of remote work and chatbots, she said, “I’ve consistently seen across my studies that introverts are even lonelier than extroverts. Even if they do prefer working alone, that doesn’t mean they don’t need other humans, and we can’t assume they’re doing fine on their own.”

When Hadley surveyed workers across all demographics to see what they wanted from their employers to feel connected, the consensus was clear. “Employees want the five to 10 minutes of meeting chit-chat, communal lunches, and the occasional team outing.” She also, however, found that the loneliest employees are also the ones usually most reluctant to engage in these team rituals. She pointed out that it’s easy to fall into a negative pattern when you’re lonely. “This is an important message for leaders to understand: It’s not an automatic “if you build it, they will come” situation. You actually need to do targeted outreach to overcome a lot of the hesitation.”

What happens when employees feel like their leaders care, and are committed to their well-being? Hadley says employees then reported higher job satisfaction, more positive attitudes towards AI, higher productivity from AI, and a stronger intention to stay at their company.

HUMAN-CENTERED LEADERSHIP

The solution is not to reject AI, but to use its efficiency to create a richer social architecture. Leaders can protect their culture by keeping vital functions—like onboarding, mentoring, conflict resolution, and performance feedback—strictly human-led. 

For Hadley, reinvesting the time saved by these AI tools back into your team is vital, especially when social isolation is believed to be the cause of so many health concerns today. The World Health Organization estimates that loneliness is associated with 100 deaths every hour. “Our lives are so digitized now that the workplace is often our only opportunity for social connection. Make it your business to invest that saved time back into your work culture. For leaders, it is a real opportunity that you are uniquely positioned to take up, and it could make a huge difference.”

Carrie Varoquiers is chief impact officer at Workday.

Goodbye, Wintel? Software for Windows too?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Huawei has introduced its first desktop PCs powered by its own 10-core processor as well as proprietary HarmonyOS operating system, reports the Southern China Morning Post. The company claims that the CPU and the OS are built entirely of using 'components manufactured' in China, which matters when it comes national security and domestic supply chains inside the sanctioned country. But whether these machines are truly 'entirely domestic' is an open question.

The Huawei Qinyun HM650 and HM650g desktop PCs come with 16 GB of LPDDR5 memory (probably made by China's CXMT) and either a 256GB or 512GB SSD (probably made by Chinese flash maker YMTC) are powered by the company's Kirin X90 system-on-chip, which originally debuted in Huawei's consumer systems in 2025. The key ingedient of the system it its processor, which features 10 Huawei-designed Armv8-based Taishan CPU cores in a 4+4+2 configuration, with all cores supporting simultaneous multithreading (SMT) to execute up to 20 threads simultameusly. The chip also integrates Huawei's Maleoon graphics processing unit (Arm Mali-based) and a dedicated neural processing unit for AI workloads.

Although Huawei doesn't officially disclose the Kirin X90's manufacturing process, a teardown analysis by TechInsights confirmed that the CPU is manufactured by SMIC using its 7nm-class N+2 process technology. This makes the X90 an example of Huawei's ability to develop PC-class processors using domestically available semiconductor manufacturing capabilities, albeit on a process technology that trails leading-edge nodes from Intel, TSMC, and Samsung.

The most interesting aspect of the Qinyun HM650 series is certainly Huawei's claim that all of its new system's components, including the processor, memory, storage, power supply, and wireless connectivity are manufactured domestically. Such certification itself does not necessarily mean that the entire semiconductor supply chain behind the machine is Chinese. While the CPU, memory, and storage chips are fabricated domestically, they are still made using foreign manufacturing equipment (from the Netherlands, U.S., and Japan), materials (from Japan), intellectual property (from the UK), and electronic design automation (EDA software from the U.S. and partly from China) tools.

Meanwhile, the claim about the operating system developed in China sounds ambitious. The machines run Huawei's HarmonyOS Enterprise Edition, which certainly reduces their dependence on foreign technology suppliers. Unlike conventional PCs that rely on Microsoft's Windows operating system, Huawei's desktops use a software platform developed and maintained by a Chinese company. Furthermore, unlike earlier HarmonyOS versions that incorporated Linux components, the HarmonyOS Enterprise Edition uses Huawei's own kernel and software architecture. This indeed gives Huawei greater control over operating system development, security updates, and integration with its hardware, although compatibility with existing Windows applications could remain a limitation for enterprise customers that rely on software by multinational corporations for Windows.

Keeping all these things in mind, can we say that Huawei's Qinyun HM650 series relies entirely on components developed and made in China? Probably yes. Yet, with major caveats, including a semiconductor supply chain that relies on tools and software designed and produced elsewhere. Furthermore, incompatibility of the OS with software designed for Windows could be a limitation for some customers.

#10548. Apple is closing the ‘world’s largest community of Apple fans.’ Why shutting it down makes sense

On Tuesday, Apple announced it will permanently shut down one of its oldest online services: the Apple Support Community forum, where users could post questions and get answers about the iPhone, the Mac, and other Apple products they owned.

The forum has existed in some form since the late ’90s, but its closure, while abrupt, makes a lot of sense. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

One Tuesday, visitors to the Apple Support Community (found at discussions.apple.com) discovered they could no longer post new topics to the nearly three-decade-old Apple forum.

Instead, they were greeted with a message from Apple announcing the community’s upcoming closure.

“The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026,” the message read. “Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.”

The message went on to thank the members of the Apple Support Community “who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.”

As of the time of this writing, all Apple Support Community posts are still available to browse, but, as Apple’s message stated, new posts cannot be created, and existing posts cannot be replied to.

And, presumably, all posts will be wiped from discussions.apple.com on November 20.

The product of a bygone era

Apple has offered some version of the Apple Support Community for nearly three decades.

As noted by 9to5Mac, in 1998, Apple launched Apple Tech Exchange, its first forum-based community support site. The purpose of the forums was to provide one central location where Apple’s customers could get their support questions answered by other Apple users.

Apple Tech Exchange eventually morphed into Apple Discussions in the early 2000s, which then became the modern Apple Support Communities in the early 2010s.

It’s unknown how many users the forums had, but even today, the portal still boasts that the Apple Support Community was “the world’s largest community of Apple fans.”

The problem with Apple Support Communities, in the opinion of many Apple users, was that the answers found on the forums were often lackluster, incomplete, or sometimes just downright wrong.

Many queries also often went unanswered, or the only replies to a tech support query were along the lines of “I’m having the same problem.”

In other words, actually getting useful help on the Apple Support Communities was often a hit-or-miss affair.

That’s not to mention that the forums were very much a product of another age. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the forums made sense as a central hub for Apple fans to share their knowledge.

But over the last 20 years, the web has changed with the rise of social media and platforms like Reddit, along with massive online communities of Apple fans that populate in MacRumors’ popular forums.

As these platforms grew more popular, Apple Support Communities became less relevant.

Why is Apple shutting down Apple Support Communities?

Beyond the message now at the top of Apple Support Communities, Apple has not publicly commented on why the forums are being shuttered. 

Fast Company has reached out to Apple for comment.

However, there are several likely reasons Apple has finally decided to close the forums.

First, this feels like some long-overdue housekeeping Apple is finally taking care of. Apple recently got a new CEO, and when new leaders come on, they tend to tidy up the place.

Second, if you spent any time on Apple Support Communities, you quickly realized that many of the people turning to the forums for help thought they were getting answers from Apple’s official support staff. However, that was never the case.

As the Apple Support Communities footer notes, the forums contained “user submitted content, comments and opinions” and were “for informational purposes only.”

Despite this disclaimer, the misconception that an Apple employee was responding to your queries seems to have been rife.

This likely led to a lot of frustration when a user found they couldn’t get a firm answer to their query, further leading to the perception that Apple’s support staff was inept—or that getting tech support from Apple was a frustrating experience. 

Those are misconceptions that Apple was probably getting sick of.

Third, as previously mentioned, web forums were all the rage in the late ’90s and early 2000s, but now if you need help with your Apple queries, the best places to get an answer quickly are usually the various tech or Apple subreddits on Reddit—or just ask the tech community that hangs out on X or Threads. 

Finally, even social media and platforms like Reddit are now being superseded by AI chatbots.

Asking ChatGPT, Gemini, or Apple’s new Siri AI how to resolve your Apple problem is often the quickest way to get a reliable answer now. (I know, shocking that AI is now superseding user-generated content.)

As for those who did find Apple Support Communities helpful, you’ve got a little over a week left to peruse the site before Apple takes it down for good on Friday, November 20.
